identifiers.title: The Effect of High-Intensity Interval Training Type on Body Fat Percentage, Fat and Fat-Free Mass: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis of Randomized Clinical Trials
identifiers.authors: Khodadadi F, Bagheri R, Negaresh R, Moradi S, Nordvall M, Camera DM, Wong A, Suzuki K
identifiers.citation: Khodadadi F, Bagheri R, Negaresh R, et al. The Effect of High-Intensity Interval Training Type on Body Fat Percentage, Fat and Fat-Free Mass: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis of Randomized Clinical Trials. J Clin Med. 2023;12(6):2291.

design.quote: This systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials (RCTs) compared body compositional changes

species.quote: These trials had a total sample size of 1130 individuals, and the mean age was 26.27 ± 5.42 years.

population.value: adults aged 18 or older without a known disease, most of them inactive and overweight or obese
population.quote: Primarily, a majority of investigations were conducted on overweight or obese inactive adults as opposed to active normal body mass or BMI adults.

sampleSize.quote: These trials had a total sample size of 1130 individuals, and the mean age was 26.27 ± 5.42 years.

facts.quote: These trials had a total sample size of 1130 individuals, and the mean age was 26.27 ± 5.42 years.

facts.label: The programme settings the authors found more effective
facts.value: training for more than 8 weeks, at least three sessions per week
facts.quote: These data suggest that training for more than 8 weeks, at least three sessions per week, lower than 60 s work intervals separated by ≤90 s recovery periods, and active rest (instead of passive) are more effective on body composition.

facts.label: An earlier meta-analysis with a different result for cycling
facts.value: found no significant effect of cycling on measures of body composition
facts.quote: a systematic review and meta-analysis by Wewege et al. [] found no significant effect of cycling on measures of body composition (whole-body FM) in overweight and obese adults

facts.label: Why running may suit heavier bodies less well
facts.quote: overweight and individuals with obesity exhibit altered joint loads, absolute ground reaction forces, and forefoot pressures compared to non-obese adults
